newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Samsung reviews Fokker proposal but no deal yet.
newsitem.headline: Samsung reviews Fokker proposal but no deal yet.

text.p: South Korea's Samsung Aerospace Industries confirmed Friday it was studying a Dutch government proposal to take over bankrupt planemaker Fokker but said no deal has been concluded.
"The Dutch government is demanding a $500 million to $600 million long-term investment in Fokker and we are favourably reviewing the proposal," a Samsung spokesman said in Seoul.
"We are undertaking negotiations with the Dutch government in a very amicable, positive manner but no agreement has been reached yet."
The Dutch government had no comment on the potential investment input cited by the spokesman or on the status of the negotiations.
Dutch news agency ANP Friday quoted a Samsung representative as saying the takeover was a done deal.
"The deal can't go wrong anymore, the only thing to be decided is when it will be announced by Samsung," the agency quoted the representative as saying.
Samsung Aerospace Industries, a unit of the giant Samsung group, wants to make use of Fokker's know-how to build a new generation of regional jets.

Court-appointed administrators who have been running Fokker since it was declared bankrupt in March gave Samsung the exclusive right to examine Fokker's books in September with a view to a possible bid for its core plane-making business.

Samsung sees a resurrected Fokker as a potential shortcut to its ambitions of becoming a major player in the global aerospace industry. But it is unwilling to assume all the risks and has sought substantial investment by the Dutch government.

The government has indicated it is willing to provide fresh capital for Fokker and invest in the development of a new 125-seat regional jet, but Samsung is said to have balked at demands for long-term job guarantees in the Netherlands.
Since March the administrators have kept the company running with a skeleton staff of 650 people.

Fokker was one of the most esteemed marques in the history of flight. Founded in 1919 by aviation pioneer Anthony Fokker, it has developed some 125 different aircraft, ranging from passenger planes to fighters and bombers.
